historical_timeline.summary: Born at Port Conway, Virginia; a frail and sickly child.
The family moves to the brick house at Montpelier, built by enslaved laborers.
College of New Jersey; graduates 1771; overwork and infirm health.
Back in Virginia, writes that he does not expect a long or healthy life.
Appointed to the Orange County Committee of Safety.
Ill health keeps him out of military service.
Virginia Convention; meets Thomas Jefferson in October.
Inherits Montpelier and more than 100 enslaved people.
Retirement: bilious fever (1821), worsening rheumatism, deafness in one ear.
Dies at Montpelier, aged 85; his will does not free the people he enslaved.
Historians and physicians propose epilepsy or other causes for his attacks; all retrospective.

claims.statement: James Madison was born at Port Conway, Virginia, on 16 March 1751 in the Gregorian calendar (5 March, Old Style), the first of twelve children of James Madison and Nelly Conway Madison; his mother was visiting her own mother's home there. A family sketch he sent in 1834 gives the date as '5th of March, 1751 (O. S.)'.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Virginia used the Julian calendar, with the legal year beginning on 25 March, until 1752; 5 March 1750/51 Old Style is 16 March 1751 Gregorian.

claims.statement: The Madison family's wealth lay in land, enslaved people, and tobacco. In the early 1760s the plantation's enslaved labor force built the brick house half a mile from the first family home, the estate later named Montpelier, in Orange County, Virginia.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented social history of the household he grew up in.

claims.statement: The Library of Congress describes him as an excellent student but a frail and sickly child. His health had always been delicate, and Williamsburg was regarded as unhealthy, which was among the reasons he went north to the College of New Jersey (Princeton) rather than to William and Mary.

He entered the College of New Jersey in 1769, graduated in 1771, and stayed on several months to study Hebrew and other subjects under John Witherspoon. His biographer Gaillard Hunt wrote that for several months he spared only three hours in twenty-four for sleep, until he found his constitution unable to endure the strain. In his own late autobiography he wrote that 'his very infirm health, had been occasioned not a little by a doubled labor', accomplishing the studies of two years in one. A later account that he was excused from the commencement exercises cannot be confirmed from the college's records.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Overwork and poor health at college are documented; their nature is not.

claims.statement: He returned to Virginia in 1772 and studied law. In November 1772 he wrote to his college friend William Bradford: 'I am too dull and infirm now to look out for extraordinary things in this world, for I think my sensations for many months have intimated to me not to expect a long or healthy life'. The Miller Center describes these as some of the most morose letters of his life, written with failing health and the expectation of an early death; Hunt describes a solitary, purposeless period darkened by enfeebled health.
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own words record poor health, low spirits, and the expectation of an early death; they do not record a diagnosis or any thought of self-harm.

source_links.locator: Chapter I, quoting Madison to William Bradford, November 1772

claims.statement: In December 1774 he was appointed to the Orange County Committee of Safety, which oversaw the county militia; he worked to build up its strength.

His health kept him from serving in the militia in the Revolution; a nineteenth-century biographer judged that his place, from temperament and want of physical vigor, was in the council, not the field.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The sources read state that ill health kept him from military service without describing the illness.

claims.statement: Later in life he suffered periodic bouts of an unknown malady that some historians, including his biographers Ralph Ketcham and Irving Brant, suspect may have been epilepsy. A physician writing in 2018 described an account of his sudden collapse at a militia drill in 1775 as an 'absence seizure' while noting that whether his later agitation came from a seizure disorder or from anxiety is not known.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective interpretations. No physician of his time recorded a diagnosis; epilepsy, functional (dissociative) seizures, anxiety, and other causes cannot be distinguished from the record.

claims.statement: In 1776, at 25, he was elected to the Virginia Convention that framed the state's constitution and met Thomas Jefferson for the first time that October. Hunt describes him then as five feet six and a quarter inches tall, thin and delicate, with a countenance that 'bespoke the suffering of bad health'.

After his presidency (1809 to 1817) there was no continuous period when his health was good. He had the prevailing bilious fever in the autumn of 1821 and recovered quickly; he suffered increasingly from rheumatism, which by his last years crippled his fingers; at 83 he was so disabled by it that he lived in one room, and he complained that one ear was deaf. His mind remained sharp.

He died at Montpelier on the morning of 28 June 1836, aged 85, the last of the Founding Fathers, extremely emaciated and growing gradually weaker; he died alone in his chair over his breakfast, minutes after his niece brought it.
claims.clinical_interpretation: No cause of death was recorded beyond weakness in old age.

claims.statement: At his father's death in 1801 he inherited Montpelier and more than 100 enslaved African Americans. He continued to hold enslaved people, became president of the American Colonization Society, and under debt sold some of them; his will did not free them but left them to his widow with the wish that they not be sold without their consent, a wish she did not honor.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Documented social history. The record gives no health information about any enslaved person.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Evaluate a 23-year-old man with two years of recurrent sudden episodes of unresponsiveness, low mood, and anxiety, already taking levetiracetam without a confirmed diagnosis: a witness-informed history, ECG and laboratory tests, brain MRI, and inpatient video-EEG monitoring to capture habitual events; a reasoned diagnosis between epilepsy, functional/dissociative seizures, and syncope at the ILAE 'documented' level of certainty; communicating the diagnosis well (ILAE task force terminology; Hall-Patch and Stone); withdrawing the unneeded antiseizure medicine; CBT-informed psychotherapy (LaFrance 1762; CODES 1768); PHQ-9 and GAD-7 measurement-based care with an SSRI by shared decision; suicide risk assessment with a safety plan and the 988 Lifeline; seizure first aid; driving under the AAN 1773 position; and planning his studies (CMID depression monograph).

hpi.narrative: Mr. Madison is seen on the morning of discharge after 72 hours of video-EEG monitoring. Two of his usual events were recorded, the second on the third evening after a night of sleep deprivation, and he confirmed on review of the video that both were typical. His MRI last week was normal. Dr. Okafor-Haverford of neurology reviewed the recordings with him yesterday and explained the diagnosis, and the neuropsychiatric assessment on the unit found generalized anxiety and a moderate depressive episode. He says he is relieved that it is not epilepsy, though he wonders how something that feels so real could come from the mind; he asked good questions and has read the written explanation. He has had no thoughts of death or self-harm, and the rifle has been locked away with the ammunition stored separately since his first visit. He has not driven since then.

assessment_plan.assessment: Both habitual events were recorded: eyes closed and resisting opening, fluctuating unresponsiveness for minutes, and slow side-to-side head movements, with a continuous normal waking EEG and no ictal or postictal change. With a typical history and normal interictal EEG and MRI, this meets the ILAE 'documented' level of certainty for functional/dissociative seizures. Epilepsy is excluded as the cause of these events: a focal impaired-awareness seizure would be expected to change the EEG, the eyes are usually open, and the events have not responded to levetiracetam. Syncope is excluded by the duration, the closed eyes, the normal ECG and orthostatic vital signs, and the normal EEG during unresponsiveness. Dr. Okafor-Haverford agrees and has explained the diagnosis to him
plan: Diagnosis explained again today in plain words and in writing: a real and common condition in which the brain switches off awareness under strain; not epilepsy and not put on; treatable
Taper levetiracetam over three weeks and stop it
CBT-informed psychotherapy, twelve weekly sessions, starting in two weeks
Keep the event diary and use the first-aid card
Do not drive yet, including during the taper
Review in six weeks

referral.question: A 23-year-old man with two years of recurrent sudden episodes of unresponsiveness, two or three a month, unchanged on levetiracetam started without an EEG, with moderate depression and anxiety. Please establish whether these are epileptic seizures, functional/dissociative seizures, syncope, or something else, ideally by capturing events on video-EEG, and advise on the antiseizure medicine, treatment, driving, and his studies
referral.urgency: Soon, within three weeks; he has stopped driving and has no suicidal thoughts
referral.pertinent_history: Mr. Madison is a 23-year-old graduate studying for the law school admission test, who finished his degree a year early and then stayed on for a year of advanced study, often sleeping five hours or less. For two years he has had sudden spells, two or three a month, in which he 'blanks out', stops speaking, and slumps or sinks to the floor with his eyes closed for two to ten minutes; he can sometimes hear voices distantly, cannot respond, and afterwards is tearful and tired. There has been no tongue biting, incontinence, or injury, and no events from sleep. The first came during examinations when he was sleeping three or four hours a night. An emergency clinician started levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily four months ago without an EEG; the events are unchanged and he has become irritable. He has low mood, worry, and a sense that he will not live long, without suicidal thoughts (PHQ-9 13, item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 14; C-SSRS screen negative). He has a hunting rifle, now locked with the ammunition stored separately, and a safety plan with the 988 Lifeline. Examination and orthostatic vital signs are normal; ECG normal with QTc 404 ms; blood count, metabolic panel, glucose, calcium, and TSH normal. A brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol is booked. I have advised him not to drive, to keep a diary, and to continue levetiracetam unchanged until your assessment
questions: Are these events epileptic, functional/dissociative, syncopal, or of another cause, and to what level of certainty?
Would you admit him for video-EEG monitoring to capture his habitual events?
Should levetiracetam be continued, changed, or withdrawn?
How should the diagnosis be explained to him?
What treatment do you recommend for the events and for his mood and anxiety?
What advice do you give on driving, safety, and his studies?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Madison is seen at the request of Dr. Pembroke-Achebe on the third day of video-EEG monitoring, and again this morning before discharge. He describes two years of spells that begin with a feeling of distance and heaviness, after which he cannot move or answer though he may hear what is said; they last two to ten minutes, end gradually, and leave him tearful and tired. There is no aura of rising sensation, déjà vu, automatisms he is aware of, tongue biting, incontinence, injury, or events from sleep. They began during a period of intense study and little sleep and are most frequent after long days. There is no history of febrile seizures, head injury, or meningitis, and no palpitations or exertional events. Levetiracetam for four months has made no difference and has made him irritable. He reports low mood and constant worry about his future and his health, without suicidal thoughts. He has not driven since his first primary care visit
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Video-EEG for 72 hours with sleep deprivation, hyperventilation, and photic stimulation, on levetiracetam: two habitual events recorded (2 minutes 40 seconds and 6 minutes), with eyes closed and resisting opening, fluctuating unresponsiveness, and slow side-to-side head movements; the EEG showed a continuous normal waking posterior rhythm during both, with no ictal or postictal change; interictal EEG normal awake and asleep; he confirmed both events as typical. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol: normal. ECG: sinus rhythm, QTc 404 ms. Blood count, metabolic panel, glucose, calcium, and TSH: normal. PHQ-9 12 and GAD-7 13 today; neuropsychiatric assessment on the unit: generalized anxiety disorder and a moderate depressive episode, without psychotic or bipolar features

assessment.assessment: Both habitual events were captured with a normal waking EEG throughout, closed and resisting eyes, and a fluctuating course: with a typical history and normal interictal EEG and MRI, this is a documented diagnosis by the ILAE criteria. I find no evidence of epilepsy: focal impaired-awareness seizures of this length would be expected to change the EEG, and the events have not responded to levetiracetam. Syncope does not explain events of several minutes with closed eyes and a normal EEG. The onset under heavy study and little sleep, with anxiety and depression, fits the usual picture. I use the ILAE task force term functional/dissociative seizures with him
